title: ACGME Compliance Tools by Scheduling Use Case: 5 Options
description: Five ACGME compliance tools for residency programs, sorted by what each does with the rules: builds them in, flags violations afterwards, or reports hours.
content:
Summary

  • Creating ACGME-compliant schedules manually consumes 10-15 hours of a chief resident's time per cycle and is highly prone to error.
  • Most scheduling tools are reactive, only flagging violations after a schedule is built; a better approach is to put the rules in while the schedule is built.
  • Tools and services that build the ACGME rules in as the schedule is created take most of the "build, check, fix" cycle off the chief.
  • A managed service like Scheduling Wizard delivers finished schedules built to the rules, removing the operator burden while working alongside existing publishing platforms like Amion and QGenda.

Every year, a new chief resident inherits the same impossible task: build a schedule that satisfies dozens of overlapping ACGME rules, resident preferences, rotation requirements, and service coverage needs, usually in Excel, usually from scratch, and usually in 10-15 hours they don't have.

The frustration is real. As one resident put it in a Reddit thread on scheduling software: "Creating residency schedules in Excel is laborious and frustrating." Another noted that their program stuck with Excel purely "so that we would have residents from each year who understood scheduling", institutional knowledge held together by tribal memory rather than any real system.

But here's the issue most programs miss: not all "ACGME compliance tools" solve the same problem.

A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

The Important Distinction: Catching Violations vs. Preventing Them

There are two different types of tools in this space, and which category a tool falls into determines whether ACGME duty hour violations get caught before or after a schedule is published.

Monitoring and Reporting Tools (Reactive): You or your chief resident builds the schedule by hand, and the tool flags the ACGME violations it detects. The burden of fixing those violations (and rebuilding the schedule) still falls entirely on you. QGenda, Amion, and New Innovations all fall into this category to varying degrees.

"Rules Built In" Tools (Proactive): This newer category doesn't just check compliance; it builds the rules into the schedule from the very first assignment. ACGME rules are built into the schedule as it is created, so the rules are applied as it is built, not just flagged after the fact.

This distinction is the crux of whether your program is playing defense or offense for compliance. With that framework in mind, here are five options, ordered by who builds the schedule.

1. Scheduling Wizard, Best for Having the Schedule Built With the Rules In

Category: Rules Built In / Done-for-You Managed Service

Scheduling Wizard is a YC-backed (W26) managed scheduling service built for residency and fellowship programs, provider groups and practices. Unlike every other tool on this list, it isn't software you log into; it's a done-for-you service. Programs submit their rules (rotation requirements, call rules, vacation requests, subspecialty-specific ACGME rules), and our team delivers the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, ready for your existing publishing platform.

What it does:

  • Builds complete Block, Clinic, Call, and Attending schedules with the ACGME requirements built in, including the subspecialty requirements you tell us apply
  • Takes the operator burden off the program: chief residents submit rules and receive a finished schedule, with no software learning curve
  • Solves the institutional knowledge problem, because your program's written rule set lives with us; it doesn't walk out the door when the chief rotates out
  • Fits existing workflows: the output is delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, and goes into whatever platform you already use for day-to-day viewing
  • Handles redrafts for bigger changes, and cross-schedule dependencies in the build

What it does not do:

  • It is not a self-service platform; you won't log in and drag shifts around yourself
  • It is not a schedule viewing or communication tool; that function is handled by your existing Amion or QGenda setup

Best for: Residency and fellowship programs that want the time sink of manual schedule creation taken off their plate, programs with complex subspecialty scheduling needs, and any department struggling with the annual loss of scheduling expertise during chief resident turnover. Programs currently using Amion or QGenda don't need to switch: Scheduling Wizard handles creation, and those tools continue to handle viewing.

What you get: finished block, call, clinic and attending schedules in the format your program wants, as Excel or Google Sheets, with a custom live view if you want one. Major redrafts through the year are included. For the specifics, see our page on ACGME compliant scheduling.

2. Excel / Google Sheets, Best for Expressing Rules No Platform Will Model

Category: Manual

Every tool on this list is competing with a spreadsheet, not with each other, so it belongs at number two. A spreadsheet will carry any requirement you can state, including the local ones that are not in any rulebook: the attending who does not take Friday calls, the rotation that two residents cannot share. No configuration screen will accept some of those. A cell will.

On ACGME specifically it offers nothing. It does not know the 80-hour average, the rest interval or the one-in-seven rule, and it will not look for them. Everything the rest of this list takes on is a person's job here, done at the end of a clinical day.

Before you compare the automation claims. Ask what the output looks like on day one and who fixes it. A generated schedule that needs a long manual pass, with each change rippling into the next, is closer to the spreadsheet above than to a finished schedule. The answer differs a lot by program complexity, so ask about yours.

3. QGenda, Best for Large Institutions With Dedicated Scheduling Staff

Category: Monitoring and Reporting / Advanced Self-Service Software

QGenda is one of the most powerful self-service scheduling platforms in healthcare. Large academic medical centers use it to manage scheduling across dozens of departments, with deep integrations into hospital HR and payroll systems.

What it does:

  • Provides a sophisticated, rules-based scheduling interface where administrators can encode complex scheduling logic
  • Offers compliance tracking that flags potential duty hour violations within a schedule after it has been built or edited
  • Integrates with enterprise systems at a scale that few other tools can match
  • Gives visibility across large organizations with multi-department reporting

What it does not do:

  • It does not build a compliant schedule for you. A user must manually construct the schedule, and QGenda will flag violations, but fixing them is still your job. As one EM resident noted in a Reddit thread on residency shift scheduling, "setting up the scheduling software is a slow and mistake-prone process." QGenda's power comes with a steep learning curve
  • The compliance burden remains high on the chief resident or coordinator responsible for building and maintaining the schedule

Best for: Large academic medical centers and health systems with dedicated administrative staff or full-time schedulers who have the bandwidth to master QGenda's configuration and ongoing management. Not ideal for programs where the chief resident is the primary scheduler.

4. Amion, Best for Schedule Viewing and Communication

Category: Publishing Platform

Amion has been a staple of residency programs for decades, and its staying power is a testament to one thing it does exceptionally well: making schedules easy to view and share.

What it does:

  • Provides a clean, universally recognized interface for publishing on-call and daily schedules that residents can access from any device
  • Allows manual schedule entry and basic edits
  • Serves as a reliable communication layer between schedulers and residents

What it does not do:

  • It has no automated ACGME compliance features. All duty hour checks must be performed manually by the scheduler, traditionally in a separate spreadsheet. This places a very high compliance burden on whoever is building the schedule, and that person is almost always the chief resident
  • It is not designed to build a complex schedule or catch conflicts

Best for: Programs that need a straightforward, widely understood tool for publishing a schedule that has already been built elsewhere. Amion is a good endpoint for a schedule built elsewhere, by a service like ours; the two are complementary.

5. New Innovations, Best for Integrated Residency Program Management

Category: Monitoring and Reporting / Residency Management Suite

New Innovations is less of a pure scheduling tool and more of a complete residency management platform. For programs that need to manage evaluations, procedure logs, curriculum, and scheduling in one place, it offers genuine value.

What it does:

  • Integrates scheduling with the broader educational and administrative infrastructure of a residency program
  • Tracks and reports on duty hours from an existing schedule, helping programs document compliance for accreditation purposes
  • Manages evaluations, milestones, case logs, and other ACGME reporting requirements alongside scheduling data

What it does not do:

  • Like QGenda, it does not proactively generate a compliant schedule. Compliance monitoring is reactive, the schedule is built first, and then hours are tracked and reported against it
  • The scheduling module is not its core strength; it functions as a component of a broader suite rather than a strong scheduler

Best for: Programs seeking a single platform to manage all aspects of residency education, administration, and compliance reporting, particularly those that prioritize having one source of truth for ACGME documentation. If pure scheduling efficiency is the primary goal, it's best paired with a dedicated schedule creation solution.

Decision Matrix: Which Tool Removes the Burden?

Use this matrix to quickly match your program's situation to the right tool. Pay close attention to the compliance method and chief resident burden columns, that's where the real difference lies.

A study published in Neurosurgery found that a rebuilt call schedule reduced call variation by 70% and improved perceived fairness from 43% to 95%, directly addressing the "extreme inequality in the scheduling system" that residents frequently cite as a primary frustration.

Tool Compliance Approach ACGME Compliance Method Chief Resident Burden
Scheduling Wizard Rules Built In Built into the schedule None
QGenda Monitoring & Reporting User-managed (flags errors post-build) High
Amion Monitoring & Reporting None (fully manual check required) Very High
New Innovations Monitoring & Reporting User-managed (tracks and reports hours) High

The pattern is clear: every monitoring and reporting tool still leaves the hardest work, building the schedule correctly in the first place, on the shoulders of your chief resident. The compliance question is whether the rules went into the build, not just whether a tool catches violations after the fact.

Where the Rules Should Go In

Most programs approach ACGME compliance as a review step: build the schedule, then check for violations, then fix and rebuild. That loop eats 10–15 hours per scheduling cycle, creates stress for chief residents who are already stretched thin, and resets entirely every time a new chief takes over.

The more effective approach is to move compliance upstream, into the schedule creation process itself, where the rules are applied rather than corrected afterward.

Tools like QGenda, Amion, and New Innovations have genuine value, especially for publishing schedules, enterprise reporting, and program-wide administration. But none of them solve the core problem of creating a compliant schedule without burdening the chief resident with that responsibility.

That's exactly the gap Scheduling Wizard was built to fill, not as a replacement for the tools your program already uses, but as the team that builds the schedule, which makes those tools easier to use by giving them a finished schedule to work with from day one.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does "rules built in" scheduling work?

The ACGME rules are written down first, alongside the program's own rules, and the schedule is built to satisfy all of them at once rather than checked against them afterwards. A review at the end still has a place; it just has far less to find, and the "build, check, fix, rebuild" cycle mostly stops.

Does Scheduling Wizard handle subspecialty-specific ACGME rules?

You tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and anything your specialty's Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you alongside your own rules before the first build. They go into the schedule while it is built rather than being flagged afterwards. We do not assume we know your requirements better than you do; we ask.

Do I need to stop using Amion or QGenda to use Scheduling Wizard?

No. It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep Amion or QGenda for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

Did the February 2026 ACGME revision change the work hour rules?

Less than the headlines suggested. The February 2026 interim revision did not change the work hour limits; it suspended enforcement of a few requirements while the ACGME prepares a larger revision, proposed to take effect in July 2028. The rules a schedule is built to today are the ones in place since 2017. We build to the rules in force, and when they change we rebuild to the new ones. The full list is in ACGME Duty Hour Rules Every Residency Schedule Must Follow.

How much time can our program save by using a managed scheduling service?

Chiefs describe 10 to 15 hours of manual work for each major scheduling period (block, call or clinic), and that time goes to the service. By outsourcing the creation process to a managed service like Scheduling Wizard, the time spent on data entry, rule-checking and revisions goes to the service. This frees up the chief resident to focus on higher-value educational and leadership responsibilities.

What is the process for getting a schedule created with Scheduling Wizard?

The process is designed to be simple and hands-off for your program. First, you submit your program's rules, including rotation requirements, call rules, vacation requests, and any specific ACGME rules. Our team then builds the schedule to them and delivers it as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, ready for review and for your publishing platform.

Is a schedule built to written rules fair to residents?

It can be. A 2024 study in Neurosurgery found that a rebuilt call schedule reduced call variation by 70% and improved residents' perception of fairness from 43% to 95%. Built this way, the schedule rests on written rules and equitable distribution, reducing the room for unintentional bias that can occur in manual processes.
